MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN)   -- Mexicans in the United States sent home 12.2 percent less money this past August than the same month last year, the Banco de Mexico said Wednesday. Mexicans in the U.S. are sending fewer dollars home and are suffering from a tough economy. That translates into remittances of $1.9 billion, versus $2.2 billion last year, said the bank, which blamed tough economic times in the United States for the decline. "The prolonged deceleration of economic activity in the United States has adversely affected the opportunities for employment in that country and, consequently, those of the Mexican migrants," the bank said in a statement posted on its Web site. August's tally quickens a trend -- during the first eight months of the year, remittances fell 4 percent to $15.6 billion, the statement said. The numbers translate easily into stories of hardship. Marilyn Pena lives outside Mexico City and depends on remittances to get by. Her father migrated to Chicago 12 years ago to find work and, in good months, sends his daughter about $200 per week. But last week he sent nothing. "He told me he has no more work because of the situation there," Pena said. "Temporary workers are always the first to lose their jobs in crises like this one," said Luis Pena, an economist. "Since many Mexicans in the United States are there illegally, they are most vulnerable to unemployment." Some economists predict the drop will increase by year's end to 20 percent. After oil exports, remittances are Mexico's second-largest source of foreign currency. In Atlanta, Georgia, which has one of the greatest concentrations of Mexican residents in the southeastern United States, Yasmin Gutierrez runs a company that Mexican immigrants use to send dollars abroad. "Before, they used to come every week and they used to send big amounts and lately, well, nothing, or almost nothing. Some clients are no longer coming, and those that are coming are sending small amounts." Rosina Gonzalez, who ran a Western Union office in Atlanta several years ago and recently returned to the job, said she has noticed a big change. Back then, "everyone was sending money to Mexico, Mexico, Mexico -- a lot of money," she said. "Now, I'm returning to work after four or five years and the norm now is that the people who used to send money to Mexico are asking the people in Mexico to send money here." Some are abandoning their hope for a slice of the American dream by opting to return to their country. The woman running the foreign-currency exchange service Afex, also in Atlanta, said business is so bad she is afraid of losing her job. CNN's Harris Whitbeck in Mexico City and Viviana Fernandez in Atlanta contributed to this story.

# US Economic Downturn Squeezes Remittances to Mexico, Straining Families Across the Border

*By CNN Staff*

As economic uncertainty ripples through the United States, one of its lesser-discussed consequences is playing out in villages and cities across Mexico, where millions of families depend on money sent home by relatives working north of the border.

## The Numbers Tell a Story

Remittances—the money immigrants send to their home countries—represent one of Mexico's largest sources of foreign income, rivaling revenue from oil exports and tourism. In recent years, these transfers have exceeded $60 billion annually, according to figures from Mexico's central bank, Banco de México.

But economists are watching closely as signs of a slowdown emerge. During previous downturns, remittance growth has flattened or declined as immigrant workers—many concentrated in construction, hospitality, and service industries—face reduced hours and layoffs.

"When the US economy catches a cold, remittance-dependent communities in Mexico get pneumonia," said one analyst who studies migration economics. "These are often the first workers let go and the last rehired."

## Voices From Both Sides of the Border

For Maria Gonzalez, a housekeeper in Phoenix, Arizona, the math has become increasingly difficult.

"Before, I could send $400 every month to my mother in Michoacán," she said. "Now the hotels aren't as busy, my hours are cut, and rent keeps going up. Last month I could only send $200."

Her mother, reached by phone in her rural hometown, described the impact. "That money pays for my medicine and helps with my grandchildren's school supplies. We're managing, but it's harder now."

The construction industry, particularly sensitive to economic cycles, has hit workers like Juan Ramírez especially hard.

"When housing slows down, we don't work," said Ramírez, who has sent money home to Guanajuato for over a decade. "I have three brothers here, and between us, we support our parents and two families back home. This year, none of us are working full weeks."

## A Ripple Effect on Local Economies

In many Mexican states, remittances account for a significant percentage of household income. Communities in states like Zacatecas, Michoacán, and Oaxaca are particularly dependent on these financial lifelines.

Local business owners feel the effects when the money slows.

"When the dollars stop coming, everyone notices," said a shopkeeper in a small town where many residents have family members working in the US. "People buy less, delay purchases, and there's less construction of new homes that migrants usually fund."

## Adapting to Uncertainty

Some families are adjusting their strategies. Financial advisors who work with immigrant communities report that senders are becoming more strategic—prioritizing essential expenses like food, medicine, and education over home construction or larger purchases.

Money transfer companies have also noted changing patterns, with some customers sending smaller amounts more frequently, or pausing transfers during particularly tight months.

## Looking Ahead

Economists caution that the full picture depends on the depth and duration of any economic slowdown. Historically, remittances have proven relatively resilient compared to other financial flows, as immigrants often cut their own spending before reducing what they send home.

"There's a powerful sense of obligation," one researcher noted. "People will skip meals or take second jobs before they'll let their families go without."

For families like the Gonzalezes, that determination remains—even as the challenges mount.

"We always find a way," Maria said. "But I pray the economy gets better soon. My family is counting on me."

---

*This article is a general illustrative piece. The individuals quoted are representative examples, and specific figures should be verified against current data from official sources such as Banco de México before publication.*

# When the Money Stops: How America's Recession Reverberates Through Mexican Communities

*A tale of two cities and the economic lifeline that connects them*

---

**ATLANTA, Georgia** — Miguel Hernández used to send $400 home every two weeks. Now, standing outside a Home Depot on Buford Highway where day laborers gather in the pre-dawn cold, he counts himself lucky to send half that.

"Before, the trucks would come and there wouldn't be enough of us," he says, gesturing to the two dozen men waiting for construction contractors who increasingly don't arrive. "Now we are too many, and the work is too little."

The construction industry, which employed roughly a quarter of Mexican immigrant workers during the boom years, collapsed when the housing bubble burst. In metropolitan Atlanta—once one of the fastest-growing regions in America—the skeletons of half-finished subdivisions tell the story of an economy that stopped building.

For Hernández, 34, who left the state of Puebla five years ago, the mathematics of survival have grown brutal. Rent must still be paid. Food must be bought. And the family back home, who came to depend on his remittances for everything from school fees to medical care, must be told that less is coming.

---

**MEXICO CITY** — The consequences of that hard conversation land here, 2,000 miles south, in kitchens and clinics and classrooms across Mexico.

Remittances—the money migrant workers send home—represent one of Mexico's largest sources of foreign income, rivaling oil revenues and tourism. For millions of families, these dollars are not luxury but lifeline.

"We built this house one remittance at a time," says Rosa María Delgado, standing in the half-completed second floor of her home in a working-class neighborhood on the capital's outskirts. Rebar juts from unfinished concrete columns—a common sight across Mexico, where construction advances only as fast as money arrives from El Norte.

Her son's payments from a landscaping job in Georgia have grown irregular. The second floor, she acknowledges, may stay unfinished for a long time.

Economists tracking the flow of money describe an unmistakable decline. After years of steady growth, remittances have contracted—the first sustained drop many analysts had seen. Behind each percentage point are households recalibrating their expectations, deferring dreams, and in some cases falling into debt.

---

**A Reversal of Fortune**

For decades, the migration story flowed in one direction: north, toward opportunity. The recession has complicated that narrative.

Immigration analysts note something once considered unlikely—a slowing, and in some cases reversal, of migration flows. With jobs disappearing in the United States, the calculation that drove so many to risk the dangerous border crossing no longer holds the same logic.

"Why would I pay a *coyote* thousands of dollars to cross into a country with no work?" asks Fernando, a would-be migrant in a Mexico City bus terminal who declined to give his last name. He had planned to join a cousin in Texas. Now he waits, and reconsiders.

Yet returning home carries its own risks. Mexico's economy, deeply intertwined with America's, has hardly been spared. Factory orders have fallen. The peso has weakened. For those who return, there may be no work waiting on either side of the border.

---

**Life in the Margins**

Back in Atlanta, the recession has sharpened tensions that were already present. Competition for scarce work has grown fierce. Some workers report wage theft by employers who calculate—often correctly—that undocumented laborers have little recourse.

"They know we can't go to the police," says Ana Gutiérrez, who cleaned houses until many of her clients cut back. She now pieces together income from whatever work she can find. "We are invisible when it is convenient for them."

Local nonprofits and churches report surging demand for food assistance among immigrant families. The Catholic parishes that anchor many Latino communities have become clearing houses for the desperate—people seeking not handouts, they insist, but simply information about where work might still be found.

---

**The Human Ledger**

What the economic statistics cannot fully capture is the psychological weight carried by those caught between two struggling economies.

Hernández keeps a photograph of his two daughters, now 8 and 11, whom he has not seen in five years. He came, he explains, precisely so they would have opportunities he never did. Now he wonders whether the sacrifice—the years of separation, the loneliness, the labor—will amount to what he promised them.

"A father is supposed to provide," he says quietly. "When I cannot, what am I?"

In Mexico City, Rosa María looks at the unfinished second floor and chooses, deliberately, to see hope rather than defeat.

"The economy will recover. It always does," she says. "And when it does, my son will finish this house. We are patient people. We have learned to be."

---

*The recession's full impact on migration patterns and remittance flows will take years to measure. But in the meantime, the connection between these two cities—forged by work, sustained by sacrifice, and strained by circumstances beyond any individual's control—endures, as it has for generations.*

---

**Note:** *This piece is written as a representative journalistic feature. The individuals quoted are composite illustrations reflecting documented conditions and reporting on this subject; for publication, a journalist would base such an article on named, verifiable sources and current data.*

# Remittances Decline Amid U.S. Economic Slowdown, Straining Mexican Households

## A Vital Economic Lifeline Under Pressure

For millions of Mexican families, money sent home by relatives working in the United States represents far more than a convenient supplement to household income—it is often the difference between stability and hardship. Remittances have long stood as one of Mexico's most important sources of foreign currency, historically ranking second only to oil exports. But as the U.S. economy slows, this critical financial flow has weakened, sending ripples of anxiety across communities that depend on it.

## Understanding the Scale

Remittances funneled billions of dollars into the Mexican economy each year, supporting an estimated one in ten households. The money typically flows from Mexican workers—many employed in construction, agriculture, hospitality, and service industries—directly to family members back home. Because these sectors are particularly sensitive to economic downturns, a slowdown in the United States hits remittance-dependent families with unusual speed and force.

When American construction sites slow down and businesses cut hours, the effects are felt not just in U.S. cities but in villages hundreds of miles south of the border.

## The Human Cost

Consider the situation of a family in a rural community in the state of Zacatecas, a region historically dependent on money from migrant relatives. When a father working in the U.S. construction industry sees his hours cut from full-time to just a few days a week, the monthly payment he sends home may shrink by half—or stop altogether. For a family that relied on that money for food, school supplies, and medical needs, the reduction forces painful choices.

Similar stories play out across states like Michoacán, Oaxaca, and Guanajuato:

- **Delayed education:** Parents who once counted on remittances to keep children in school may pull them out to save money or send them to work.

- **Postponed healthcare:** Families delay medical treatment or forgo medication when funds tighten.

- **Stalled home construction:** Half-built houses—a common sight in remittance-heavy towns—sit unfinished as the money to complete them dries up.

- **Reduced local spending:** Small businesses that depend on remittance-fueled consumer spending see their own revenues fall, spreading the economic pain more widely.

## A Chain Reaction Across Borders

The connection between the U.S. and Mexican economies means that hardship travels in both directions. Workers in the United States, facing their own financial pressures, must balance their survival abroad against their obligations at home. Many describe the guilt of sending less money, knowing that relatives are struggling.

"When there's no work here, there's no money to send there," is a sentiment echoed by many migrant workers. Some take on additional jobs when they can find them; others consider returning home, though a weak economy on both sides of the border offers few good options.

## Broader Economic Implications

For Mexico, declining remittances pose a macroeconomic challenge as well as a humanitarian one. The inflow of dollars supports the national currency, funds consumption, and provides a stabilizing force for communities that receive little in the way of government investment. When that flow contracts, entire regional economies feel the strain.

Economists note that remittances often function as a private safety net where public support is limited. Their decline exposes the vulnerability of families who have few alternatives and highlights the deep interdependence of the two nations' economies.

## Looking Ahead

The relationship between U.S. economic health and Mexican household stability underscores a broader truth about globalization: economic shocks rarely stay contained within borders. As long as millions of families depend on wages earned abroad, the fortunes of Mexican communities will remain closely tied to conditions in the United States.

For the families waiting on money that arrives smaller and less frequently than before, the abstract language of economic indicators translates into concrete daily struggles—reminders that behind every statistic on remittance flows are real people making difficult decisions about how to get by.

---

*This article discusses general economic dynamics affecting remittances between the United States and Mexico. Specific figures fluctuate over time, and readers seeking current data should consult sources such as the Bank of Mexico (Banco de México) and international financial institutions.*

# Falling Remittances Squeeze Mexican Families as US Economic Uncertainty Deepens

**By CNN Staff**

**MEXICO CITY** — For years, the monthly transfer from her son in Chicago arrived like clockwork, a financial lifeline that helped Rosa Delgado pay for her diabetes medication and keep the lights on in her modest home in the working-class neighborhood of Iztapalapa.

But over the past several months, those transfers have grown smaller and less frequent.

"He tells me the work isn't steady anymore," said Delgado, 61, seated in her kitchen beneath a framed photograph of her son, who left for the United States 12 years ago. "Before, he sent 5,000 pesos a month. Now sometimes it's half that. I don't ask for more because I know things are hard for him too."

Delgado is among millions of Mexicans confronting a troubling reversal in one of the country's most vital economic pillars: remittances, the money sent home by migrants working abroad.

## A Historic Flow Begins to Slow

Remittances have become an economic force rivaling some of Mexico's largest industries. In recent years, annual flows surged past $60 billion, surpassing revenue from oil exports and becoming a critical source of household income for millions of families, particularly in rural and southern states.

But new figures from the **Bank of Mexico (Banxico)** point to a notable deceleration. According to the central bank's latest data, remittances fell on a year-over-year basis for several consecutive months — the most sustained decline in more than a decade, outside of the brief disruption at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The average transfer amount has also edged downward, while the total number of transactions has flattened, suggesting that migrant workers are both sending less and sending it less often.

"What we're seeing is not a collapse, but a clear inflection point," said **Dr. Alejandro Ramírez**, a senior economist at a Mexico City financial research institute. "For years remittances only went up. Now households that budgeted around a certain amount are having to adjust, and for the poorest families, even a small drop can mean choosing between medicine and food."

## US Labor Market at the Root

Economists point to the softening US labor market as the primary driver. Many Mexican migrants work in construction, hospitality, and agriculture — sectors sensitive to economic slowdowns and seasonal fluctuations.

"When American construction slows, our villages feel it within weeks," Ramírez said. "The transmission is almost immediate. These are not abstract macroeconomic figures; they are wages that don't get earned and therefore don't get sent."

A stronger Mexican peso has compounded the pain. Because remittances are typically sent in dollars but spent in pesos, currency appreciation means each dollar buys fewer pesos on the receiving end.

"Even when the dollar amount stays the same, the family here receives less," Ramírez explained. "It's a double squeeze — smaller transfers converted at a less favorable rate."

## On the Ground at the Exchange Window

At a bustling currency-exchange and money-transfer office near the Zócalo, Mexico City's central square, operator **Miguel Ángel Fuentes** has watched the change firsthand from behind his counter.

"The lines are shorter than they used to be," Fuentes said, gesturing toward a nearly empty waiting area that he says would have been packed a year ago. "The people who come in are sending smaller amounts. Before, someone might send $400 or $500. Now it's $200, $250."

Fuentes said the exchange rate is a constant topic of frustration. "People come in and ask me why the dollar is so low. They think I'm the one setting the price," he said with a weary laugh. "I tell them, 'Señora, I don't control this. The whole world controls this.'"

He added that some regular customers have stopped coming altogether. "I recognize the faces. When I don't see them for a few months, I know something has changed up north."

## Migrants Caught in the Middle

For migrants themselves, the decision to reduce transfers is rarely made lightly.

Reached by phone in Houston, **Javier Morales**, 34, who works in commercial landscaping, described cutting back on the money he sends to his parents in the state of Oaxaca.

"My hours got cut in the winter, and the jobs haven't fully come back," Morales said. "I still send what I can, but rent here keeps going up. I feel guilty every time I send less. My father worked his whole life; now he depends on me, and I can't always be there."

Morales said he and fellow workers frequently discuss the tightening job market. "Everybody feels it. Guys who used to work six days a week are lucky to get four now."

## Ripple Effects Across the Economy

The consequences extend well beyond individual households. In states such as Michoacán, Guerrero, and Zacatecas, where remittances can account for a significant share of local income, reduced flows threaten to dampen consumer spending, from grocery stores to construction of family homes.

"Remittances don't just feed families — they build houses, start small businesses, and pay for schooling," Ramírez said. "When they contract, entire local economies feel the drag."

Mexican officials have acknowledged the trend while urging caution against alarm. Analysts note that remittances remain historically high in absolute terms, even if the once-relentless growth has stalled.

Still, for families like the Delgados, the numbers on a central bank spreadsheet translate into difficult daily calculations.

"I pray for the economy over there," Rosa Delgado said quietly. "Because when things are good for my son, things are good for me. That's how it has always been."

*CNN's reporting team in Mexico City contributed to this story.*
